items.title: [ft.com] Britain’s grid operator issues record number of power alerts as wind bottlenecks persist
items.content_html: Britain’s National Energy System Operator issued electricity margin notices on three consecutive days, Nov. 24-26, as transmission limits restricted wind power from Scotland and colder weather increased demand. On Nov. 26, notices cited a 1.3-gigawatt shortfall in the morning and nearly 2.8 gigawatts later in the day. The operator said the notices were precautionary and did not signal a risk of power cuts. In Brazil, almost 22% of potential wind and solar output was curtailed between January and September. Wind utility Copel has paused new wind investments after curtailment cut its quarterly operating profit. Britain’s notices followed maintenance that left the B4 transmission boundary, linking northern and southern Scotland, operating at about half its 3.4-gigawatt capacity. Brazil’s first battery-storage auction is scheduled for early December, with contracts due to begin in 2028.

items.title: [list.solar] Ireland awards 1,555 MW of renewables, mostly solar, in auction
items.content_html: Ireland’s sixth Renewable Electricity Support Scheme (RESS) auction provisionally awarded 1,367.25 MW of solar and 188.05 MW of onshore wind across 28 projects, according to results published by grid operator EirGrid on Nov. 25. The solar awards total about 30% of the gap between Ireland’s nearly 3.5 GW of installed solar capacity and its 8 GW target. Bidders can file notices of dissatisfaction through Nov. 27. EirGrid expects to publish final results, subject to ministerial approval, on Dec. 9, with award notices scheduled for Jan. 11, 2027.

items.title: [pv-magazine-india.com] India rooftop solar additions reach 11.2 GW through September
items.content_html: India added 11.2 GW of rooftop solar capacity in the first nine months of 2026, a 129% increase from 4.9 GW in the same period last year, according to Mercom India’s market report. Cumulative rooftop capacity reached 32 GW by Sept. 30. Residential systems accounted for about 9.9 GW of the nine-month additions. The government’s PM Surya Ghar program had enabled nearly 5.95 million households to install rooftop solar by September, while another 3.7 million applications remained pending. The program is scheduled to end in March 2027. Mercom Capital Group CEO Raj Prabhu said faster financing and smoother utility processes were needed to turn pending applications into installations.

items.title: [voiceofrenewables.com] GreenIT starts construction of 131 MW solar plant in Sicily
items.content_html: Italian renewable-energy joint venture GreenIT began building a 131-megawatt solar plant near Assoro in Sicily on Nov. 26. The project is its largest solar facility in Italy, and Circet Italia is the builder. GreenIT expects the plant to begin operating by the end of 2028 and produce about 210 gigawatt-hours of electricity annually. The facility will use about 205,000 bifacial photovoltaic modules on fixed-tilt structures. GreenIT, owned 51% by Plenitude and 49% by CDP Equity, is pursuing a 1-gigawatt renewables target. Its deadline for reaching that target has shifted from 2025 to 2027 and then to 2030.

items.title: [mercomindia.com] Battery maker Fluence posts $274 million loss as backlog surges
items.content_html: U.S. battery-storage company Fluence reported a record $8.9 billion order backlog at the end of its fiscal year on Sept. 30, 2026, and a net loss of $273.9 million. Annual revenue rose 3.1% to $2.33 billion. Delays in increasing production at a contract manufacturing facility in Houston held back project shipments; Fluence incurred about $90 million in related penalties and $85 million in manufacturing and equipment cost overruns. Fluence said Houston output had risen from about three units a day in early September to 10 units a day, and that most planned automation improvements were in place. The company deferred its fiscal 2027 financial guidance until its first-quarter earnings call in February 2027, as management works on production planning, pricing and costs.

items.title: [wral.com] November supermoon coincided with record California tides, flooding waterfronts
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Nov. 24 Beaver supermoon coincided with record-high tides along parts of California’s coast, where flooding affected low-lying waterfront communities in the San Francisco Bay Area and heavy surf destroyed a popular pier. The moon was full near its closest point to Earth in its monthly orbit, adding to the gravitational effects that produce higher high tides and lower low tides when the sun, Earth and moon align. When a full moon’s alignment with the sun and Earth occurs near lunar perigee, spring tides can be amplified; these tides are often called king tides. The report links the coastal impacts to the timing of the lunar event but does not identify the pier or give a flooding total. WRAL lists two International Space Station (ISS) viewing opportunities: a pass on Nov. 29 from about 6:55 to 6:58 p.m., and a longer pass on Nov. 30 beginning around 6:05 p.m.. During the later pass, the station is expected to remain visible for about six minutes as it travels from northwest to southeast.

items.title: [latimes.com] California king tides flood coastal homes as warming raises water levels
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Unusually warm Pacific waters and a strong El Niño raised coastal water levels as November king tides flooded California homes and streets, damaged seawalls and contributed to the collapse of part of Pacifica’s pier. Los Angeles, Santa Barbara and La Jolla set or matched tide records, while floodwaters in Pacifica overwhelmed pumps despite sandbags and other preparations. Ocean warming expands seawater, while human-caused sea-level rise raises the starting point for each tide. In San Francisco, sea level rose about 9.7 inches from 1900 to 2025, with 6.1 inches attributed to human-caused warming, Yale Climate Connections reported. California officials and coastal researchers warned that temporary barriers cannot manage repeated flooding as sea levels continue to rise. Another Pacific storm could bring heavy rain and strong winds to central California around Dec. 1, and forecasters expect further king tides in December and January.

items.title: [mercomindia.com] Suzlon begins construction of ₹2 billion blade factory in Tamil Nadu
items.content_html: Suzlon Energy has begun building a ₹2 billion ($21.55 million) wind-turbine blade factory in Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu, designed to produce enough blades annually for 1 gigawatt of turbine capacity. The company expects to add the plant’s manufacturing capacity within about 12 months and says it will make blades up to 95 meters long for its S175 5-megawatt turbine. The facility is one of three planned blade factories powered by artificial intelligence, with the other sites in Gujarat and Karnataka. The factories are intended to expand supply for Suzlon’s roughly 6-GW order book. Suzlon will fund the project with internal cash, without borrowing or a capital increase, according to the company’s filing. Suzlon expects the plant to create more than 1,000 skilled jobs, with at least 80% of workers coming from rural areas, Power Technology reported.

items.title: [pv-magazine.com] Italy awards 16 GWh of battery storage at lower auction prices
items.content_html: Italy’s grid operator Terna awarded 16 GWh of battery-storage capacity in its second MACSE procurement auction on Nov. 24, at a weighted-average premium of €11,382 per megawatt-hour-year. The premium was 12% below the first auction’s level, while bids totaled about 43 GWh for the 16 GWh sought. The winning projects must provide the contracted capacity for 15 years and are scheduled to begin operating in 2029. The auction covered southern Italy and its islands, where Terna is buying storage to shift renewable electricity to periods of demand and reduce reliance on gas-fired generation. Terna said it set the procurement volume so storage costs would be lower than the savings from reduced gas use. Developers that missed out can pursue merchant-market revenues, tolling agreements or Italy’s capacity market, though revised capacity-rating coefficients affect projects in some southern zones.

items.title: [list.solar] Greenvolt starts $120 million New Mexico solar-storage project
items.content_html: Greenvolt Power has begun construction on a 100-megawatt solar plant paired with a 50-MW, 200-megawatt-hour battery in Otero County, New Mexico, with an investment of more than $120 million. The Alamogordo project is Greenvolt Power’s largest combined solar and storage development in the United States to date, with completion expected by summer 2028. The battery can discharge at full power for four hours, shifting some solar generation to later periods. PV Magazine reports that the project has a power purchase agreement with Tri-State Generation and Transmission; financing includes a $190 million package arranged with MUFG Bank and ING Capital.

items.title: [nucnet.org] Framatome opens €100 million reactor-parts workshop in France
items.content_html:
Framatome, the nuclear engineering subsidiary of French state-owned utility Électricité de France (EDF), has opened a nearly €100 million workshop at Le Creusot in eastern France to manufacture and assemble reactor pressure-vessel internals. The facility occupies about 15,000 square metres and will supply France’s programme to build six EPR2 reactors.

Production began in July 2026, and Framatome expects the first deliveries in 2032. The components are made from nearly 7,600 pieces. The workshop has machining and welding equipment and dedicated training areas.

items.title: [ArchDaily] From Policy to Pavement: Preparing Cities for El Niño in the Greater Horn of Africa
items.content_html: To limit the toll of El Niño's October-December rains, IGAD's specialized climate institution, the Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC), has released a practical guide with UN-Habitat for Horn of Africa cities. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) is a regional bloc in Eastern Africa of governments from the Greater Horn of Africa, and their High-Level Call to Action on El Niño Preparedness establishes a regional commitment to move from reactive disaster response to proactive action for long-term resilience. Emphasizing cross-border coordination and crediting local knowledge, the call states: "We recognize that climate and disaster risks do not respect national borders, and that no single country or institution can manage them alone."

items.title: [theguardian.com] More than 120 climate scientists urge House to reject energy permitting bill
items.content_html: More than 120 climate scientists urged the U.S. House to reject a sweeping energy permitting bill that the Senate passed 62-33 on Nov. 19, warning it could lock in fossil-fuel projects while weakening environmental safeguards. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would shorten federal reviews and make it harder to challenge some projects in court; its supporters say faster approvals could help connect clean power and lower electricity costs. The House is expected to take up the measure after the Thanksgiving recess, but no vote date has been announced. Lawmakers also face year-end legislation, including government funding due by Dec. 11. If the House passes it, the bill would go to President Donald Trump, whose administration has endorsed it.

items.title: [africanews.com] DR Congo suspends cobalt exports again as prices fall
items.content_html: The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) will suspend all cobalt exports from Nov. 30 until further notice, its strategic minerals regulator, ARECOMS, announced on Nov. 23. The government says it is responding to falling prices, weak global consumption and rising inventories. The DRC supplies nearly three-quarters of the world’s cobalt, used in batteries for electric vehicles and consumer electronics. The suspension is due for review four months after it takes effect. Kinshasa previously replaced an export halt with quotas. Industry participants warn that restricting shipments may not clear the glut if copper mining continues to produce cobalt as a byproduct while demand remains weak.

items.title: [ft.com] England's 5,258 heat deaths spur calls for climate adaptation
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

An estimated 5,258 heat-associated deaths in England in summer 2026, a record, have intensified calls to prepare homes, health services and public infrastructure for rising temperatures. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) warned that climate change will make extreme heat longer, more frequent and more intense. The estimate covers May to September and remains provisional because death-registration data are incomplete. The summer was also dry: drought was declared across Wales and more than two-thirds of England, while wildfires damaged parts of the country. The agency said heat protection should start early in the season because people and public services may be less prepared for heat episodes in May and June. It also urged longer-term adaptation alongside emissions cuts.

items.title: [windpowermonthly.com] Scottish floating wind project reserves 28 Siemens Gamesa turbines
items.content_html: Green Volt, a planned floating offshore wind farm off Peterhead, Scotland, has reserved manufacturing capacity for 28 Siemens Gamesa turbines rated at more than 15 megawatts each. The project has consent for up to 560 megawatts and would supply electricity to the UK grid. The reservation is a procurement step, not a final turbine supply contract, and Siemens Gamesa says further milestones remain. Green Volt’s developers also signed a letter of intent with the Port of Aberdeen for anchor and mooring operations at Aberdeen South Harbour, supporting a proposed £15 million package for infrastructure and supply-chain work. The project secured key consents and a 400-megawatt UK government Contract for Difference in 2024, but still needs further contracts and investment before construction.

items.title: [energynews.biz] Battery developers expand four-hour storage as power markets shift
items.content_html: Battery developers are planning longer-duration projects as solar growth and rising electricity demand increase the need to shift power into evening peaks. In France, BW ESS and local developer Wattmen plan to develop about 500 megawatts of battery projects over three years, with at least four hours of storage per site. In the United States, utility-scale battery capacity reached nearly 52 gigawatts by June 2026. U.S. developers are competing with gas peaker plants, while French batteries could earn revenue from wholesale power, balancing services and capacity markets. Japan’s storage market faces uncertainty over whether strong early revenues from ancillary services can sustain projects over their 20-year lifetimes, Umer Sadiq said.

items.title: [pv-magazine.com] Chinese maker brings foldable off-grid solar EV charger to Australia
items.content_html: Chinese portable solar equipment maker Gaotu Innovation has introduced a roof-mounted, off-grid electric-vehicle charger in Australia that combines a foldable solar array with up to 1,600 watts of input and a 2.5-kilowatt-hour battery. Gaotu says the system can provide up to 80 kilometres of daily driving range without grid power and is aimed at drivers travelling in remote areas or camping. The company says the battery buffers solar input and supplies regulated alternating-current power to a vehicle. The unit can also provide backup power during mains outages. Gaotu offers the system to Australian distributors and says it can customize versions for local partners.

items.title: [ArchDaily] COP31 in Antalya: What the Climate Summit Means for Buildings and Cities
items.content_html: The 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) concluded on November 22, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, following negotiations that extended beyond the scheduled closing date. Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading the negotiations, the summit brought together representatives of nearly 200 Parties, alongside researchers, businesses, climate organizations, and civil society, to advance international climate action. While countries reached decisions on climate finance, adaptation, just transition, and other agenda items, they failed to agree on the proposed overarching Antalya Pact, with disagreements over fossil fuels, finance, and the level of ambition in the final text. For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] America is building just 10% of the power lines it needs, experts warn
items.content_html: America’s power grid is falling dangerously behind as electricity demand skyrockets, fueled by data centers, electric vehicles, and industry. The U.S. is building only 10% of the new high-voltage transmission lines experts say it needs, threatening higher energy prices and greater blackout risks. Researchers argue that political obstacles and outdated regulations, rather than technological limitations, are the real problem.

items.title: [solarquarter.com] SJVN brings 45 MW of Assam solar project online; ACME Solar wins 50 MW deal
items.content_html: India’s SJVN has begun commercial operations for 45 MW of its 50 MW Sonitpur solar project in Assam, while ACME Solar secured a separate 50 MW renewable-power contract in Gujarat at Rs 4.58 per kWh. The 45 MW portion passed its trial run on Nov. 21 and supplies power to Assam Power Distribution Co. under a 2024 agreement. SJVN has not given a date for bringing the remaining 5 MW online. ACME won its contract in Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam’s (GUVNL) auction for firm, dispatchable renewable power. The company says it will provide round-the-clock electricity from a project combining solar, wind and storage.

items.title: [wral.com] Data center power surge drives new rules and clean-energy proposals
items.content_html: Electricity demand from data centers is prompting new rules and power proposals in the United States and Europe. Researchers estimate that 403 U.S. hyperscale facilities use about 82 terawatt-hours annually—roughly 2% of national electricity sales—and emit about 26 million metric tons a year. The study estimates that data centers account for 18.6% of Oregon’s 2024 retail electricity sales, 15.5% in Virginia and 13.1% in Iowa. North Carolina adopted financial protections intended to limit the risk that households pay for infrastructure built for data centers, while commissioners in Shelby County, Tennessee, voted to regulate facilities’ energy and water use. Spain approved rules requiring data centers to match at least 80% of their hourly electricity use with newly installed renewable generation by 2032, with a phased transition. A separate proposal would use renewable power stored as heat to supply data centers with electricity, but its author said no U.S. data center is using that approach yet.

items.title: [energytracker.asia] COP31 fossil-fuel deadlock leaves energy shift to voluntary pledges
items.content_html: United Nations climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ended Nov. 22 without an overarching agreement after the European Union and several other countries rejected a draft that omitted a direct reference to moving away from fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia, Russia and other fossil-fuel-dependent states opposed such language. Delegates adopted no new overarching political direction on fossil fuels, while separate voluntary initiatives continued, including an electrification pledge backed by more than 90 countries. A proposal to expand carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) to gigatonne scale by 2035 was also disputed. Global operating capture capacity was about 68 million tonnes a year in mid-2026, while deployment across Asia remains limited. Countries adopted a three-year extension of the Just Transition Work Programme, but the mechanism intended to put it into operation remained underdeveloped. The International Maritime Organization’s 176 member states are due to discuss a shipping emissions framework on Nov. 30 that could establish global carbon pricing and binding measures.

items.title: [pv-magazine-india.com] Sterling and Wilson wins two orders, is lowest bidder for third; projects total over ₹2,050 crore
items.content_html: Sterling and Wilson Renewable Energy said on Nov. 23 it had secured two Indian renewable-energy contracts and was the lowest bidder for a third, with the three projects together valued at more than ₹2,050 crore. They include a 600 MWh turnkey battery-storage project in Gujarat and solar projects totaling 350 MW in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh. The Madhya Pradesh solar project still requires a formal contract award from the state-run buyer. The company did not identify the customers or disclose individual project values or work schedules.
